question: The recent sinking of a vessel south of Crete, with 32 dead and missing displaced persons, contradicts the claims made by the Nea Dimokratia Government about ‘control of the flows’ and the alleged success of the unacceptable measure whereby asylum procedures were suspended for three months.

These events are the norm in Greece and other countries and are the result of the EU’s reactionary strategy, which is now being stepped up with the appalling new ‘Pact on Migration and Asylum’. The transnational agreements that exist between the EU and third countries aim to further intensify the crackdown, now also featuring modern concentration camps, also known as ‘return hubs’.

At the same time, these agreements secure a rightless workforce on behalf of European business groups. The so-called Solidarity Pool is a cynical agreement between bourgeois governments to share out the crackdown at the borders. In the light of the above: 1.

What view does the Commission take of the call to ensure the rescue of all refugees in distress at sea and at border crossings and their right to asylum with safe passage to their countries of destination under the Geneva Convention relating to the Status of Refugees?

What view does it take of the fact that, under the ‘Pact on Migration and Asylum’ and its provisions on banishing refugees to concentration camps in third countries, this right is directly impacted and refugees are forced to seek out more dangerous journeys through ‘trafficking networks’, thus endangering their lives?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.3.2026) The Commission deeply deplores the tragic shipwreck south of Crete. All Member States involved in search and rescue operations must prioritise saving lives at sea, in accordance with their obligations under EU and international law. The Geneva Convention1 does not provide for a right of passage to a specific country.

EU asylum rules concern applications made within the territory, at the border, in territorial waters or in transit zones of Member States2, and therefore do not regulate situations before an applicant reaches those zones.

The Pact on Migration and Asylum3 aims to establish a comprehensive and balanced framework for migration management in the EU, combining responsibility and solidarity and ensuring full respect for fundamental rights and international obligations.

It seeks to reduce dangerous journeys, illegal migration to the EU, address migrant smuggling and trafficking networks, and ensure that persons in need of international protection have access to appropriate procedures.

The Commission proposal of March 2025 establishing a common EU system for returns4 lays down the legal base to allow a Member State to establish ‘return hubs’ in third countries, provided that international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law, including the principle of non-refoulement, are respected.
1 Convention relating to the Status of Refugees, signed in Geneva on 28 July 1951, as amended by the Protocol

relating to the Status of Refugees of 31 January 1967. 2 Article 3 of Directive 2013/32/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 June 2013 on common procedures for granting and withdrawing international protection (recast), OJ L 180, 29.6.2013, pp. 60–95. 3 https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum_en.

4 Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing a common system for the return of third-country nationals staying illegally in the Union, and repealing Directive 2008/115/EC of the European Parliament and the Council, Council Directive 2001/40/EC and Council Decision 2004/191/EC, COM/2025/101 final.
